John the Baptist
JON thuh BAP-tist
proper noun (figure)
From Hebrew Yochanan, "the LORD is gracious"; surnamed the Baptist, Greek baptistes, from baptizo, to immerse, for the baptism of repentance he administered.

See also: John the Baptist · John the Baptist

📖 Biblical Definition

John the Baptist was the forerunner of the Lord Jesus Christ, the last and greatest of the prophets of the old covenant, sent to prepare His way. He is the voice foretold by Isaiah: "The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD" (Isa 40:3), and the messenger of Malachi, "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me" (Mal 3:1). He came preaching "in the wilderness of Judaea... Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matt 3:1–2), and baptized with the baptism of repentance, requiring fruits meet for repentance and pointing beyond himself to the Lamb of God. When his disciples grew jealous for him, John spoke the model words of every true minister: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). Of him the Lord testified, "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he" (Matt 11:11) — greatest as the herald who stood at the threshold of the new covenant, yet less in privilege than the humblest believer who stands within it, knowing the finished work of Christ. He sealed his witness in martyrdom under Herod. This dictionary confesses John as the faithful forerunner whose whole greatness lay in pointing away from himself to the Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The forerunner of Christ, last of the old-covenant prophets, who preached the baptism of repentance and pointed to the Lamb of God. Christ called him the greatest born of women, yet the least in the kingdom is greater than he.

JOHN THE BAPTIST, proper noun. The forerunner of Christ and last of the prophets before the gospel.

Foretold by Isaiah and Malachi as the voice and messenger preparing the LORD's way.

"Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matt 3:2), preaching the baptism of repentance.

He pointed wholly away from himself: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30).

Christ named him greatest of those born of women, yet the least in the kingdom is greater (Matt 11:11).

📖 Key Scripture

Isa 40:3 — "The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God."

Mal 3:1 — "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts."

John 3:30 — "He must increase, but I must decrease."

Matt 11:11 — "Verily I say unto you, Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

John's witness is distorted wherever his baptism of repentance is detached from his testimony to Christ, or wherever a minister inverts his rule and seeks to increase while Christ decreases.

expand to see more

Some have made too much of the man and too little of his message, gathering as disciples of John rather than passing through him to Christ — an error already met in Acts, where men who knew "only the baptism of John" were brought on to faith in the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:3–5). John would have none of it; his whole greatness lay in self-effacement, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). The minister who builds a following to himself, who increases while Christ is obscured, has reversed the forerunner's rule and forfeited his glory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is John's model of ministry: a voice, not the Word; a friend of the Bridegroom who rejoices to hear His voice; a herald content to fade as the Sun rises. Every preacher and every saint is called to John's posture — to point away from self to the Lamb of God who taketh away the sin of the world, and to count it joy to decrease that Christ may increase.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

His name means "the LORD is gracious," and his surname, the Baptist, comes from the immersing baptism of repentance he administered.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yochanan, "the LORD is gracious," the meaning of John's name.

Greek baptistes, Baptist, from baptizo, to immerse, marks his baptism of repentance.

Isaiah's "voice... in the wilderness" (40:3) names his office as forerunner.

Malachi's "my messenger" (3:1) foretells the herald before the Lord's coming.

"He must decrease" (John 3:30) fixes his place: all greatness in pointing to Christ.

Usage

"John the Baptist cried in the wilderness, preparing the way of the Lord he was sent to herald."

"The pastor took John the Baptist as his pattern: he must increase, but I must decrease."

"Greatest of the prophets, John the Baptist still counted the least believer in the kingdom greater than he."
